overview.title: Pretraining data; pooling for classification
overview.main_topic: A sidebar on where Transformer pretraining data comes from (internet text, increasingly undisclosed), then the start of fine-tuning: reducing RoBERTa's (batch, seq_len, 768) output to one vector per review by taking the first token's representation, before adding a classification head.
overview.central_idea: Pretrained Transformers are shaped by huge and increasingly opaque web-scale datasets, so knowing a model's data matters for its biases and performance. To classify with an encoder, a sequence of contextual vectors must be pooled to one vector; using the first (`<s>`) token works slightly better than mean or max pooling because attention lets that position gather information from the whole sequence contextually.
overview.importance: The sidebar gives context about data provenance that chapter 16 builds on. The pooling decision explains the key line `x = x[:, 0, :]` in Listing 15.22 (p.485), which turns RoBERTa into an IMDb classifier.
learning_objectives: Describe how the scale of Transformer training data grew: millions → billions → trillions of tokens.
Give the pretraining data sources the book lists for the original Transformer, BERT, GPT-2 and Llama.
Explain why data provenance matters (biases, performance) and why it is increasingly undisclosed.
State the backbone's output shape and why it must be reduced before predicting a label.
Compare mean/max pooling with first-token pooling and explain why attention makes first-token pooling work.

paragraphs.excerpt: With our inputs preprocessed, we are ready to start fine-tuning our model.
paragraphs.what_it_says: The preprocessing is finished and fine-tuning can start.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The `preprocessed_*_ds` datasets from Listing 15.21 (p.483) now produce exactly the `token_ids`/`padding_mask` dicts the backbone expects. What remains is to give the backbone a task-specific head (this page and p.485) and train it.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It marks the end of the three-step recipe (load model, preprocess data, fine-tune).

terminology.meaning: Continuing to train a pretrained model, usually with a small learning rate, on a task-specific labeled dataset.

paragraphs.excerpt: Transformers are data-hungry models. They perform better the more input you throw at
paragraphs.what_it_says: Transformers perform better the more data they get, at an unprecedented scale: millions of tokens for the original Transformer, then billions, now trillions. The data comes mostly from the internet, but its exact composition is increasingly kept secret by companies.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Data scale has grown by roughly six orders of magnitude in a few years. Curated datasets (translation pairs, Wikipedia) could not supply that, so web crawls became the main source. Data has also become a competitive advantage and a legal risk (copyright, privacy), which explains the secrecy.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: The model you download (RoBERTa here) inherits the content, style and biases of its training text. When the data is undisclosed, users cannot easily audit what the model has learned or whether a benchmark leaked into its training set.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: a token is roughly 3/4 of an English word for typical subword tokenizers, so 15 trillion tokens is on the order of 10 trillion words.

terminology.meaning: The unit models are trained on, a subword piece produced by the tokenizer; dataset sizes are quoted in tokens.
The proportions of different sources (web, books, code, Wikipedia...) in a pretraining set.

paragraphs.excerpt: The very first Transformer trained on a well-known English-German translation
paragraphs.what_it_says: The original Transformer trained on a well-known English-German translation dataset with 4 million sentence pairs.
paragraphs.what_it_means: This is a supervised, parallel corpus: each English sentence is paired with its German translation, as in the English-Spanish data of this chapter. Beyond the book, it is the WMT 2014 English-German dataset, about 4.5 million sentence pairs.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It is the baseline for the growth that follows. At this stage the data was curated, public and labeled (paired).

terminology.meaning: A dataset of aligned sentence pairs in two languages.

paragraphs.excerpt: BERT used a dump of English Wikipedia plus a dataset containing 7,000
paragraphs.what_it_says: BERT trained on an English Wikipedia dump plus a dataset of about 7,000 self-published books.
paragraphs.what_it_means: This is unlabeled text, used with masked language modeling (p.479). The book dataset is BooksCorpus, whose long-form narrative text complements Wikipedia's encyclopedic style. Beyond the book: about 800M words of books and 2.5B words of Wikipedia, roughly the 16 GB cited on p.479.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It completes p.479, which said BERT drew 'for the most part' on Wikipedia. Even this modest mixture shows deliberate choices of genre.

terminology.meaning: A full export of a website's content, e.g. all Wikipedia articles at a given date.

paragraphs.excerpt: GPT2, a precursor to ChatGPT, scraped a dataset by following outgoing links
paragraphs.what_it_says: GPT-2, a precursor to ChatGPT, built its dataset by following outgoing links from Reddit.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Reddit links act as a crowd-sourced quality filter: pages people chose to share. Beyond the book: OpenAI's WebText kept links with at least 3 karma, giving about 8 million documents (~40 GB).
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It marks the move to web-scale scraping with heuristic quality filters, and shows how a data-collection choice imports a community's interests and biases into a model.

terminology.meaning: Automatically downloading and extracting text from web pages.

connections: Chapter 16: decoder-only GPT-style models and the role of data mixtures

paragraphs.excerpt: The latest version of Llama, a pretrained Transformer released by Meta, is
paragraphs.what_it_says: The latest Llama (from Meta) was trained on "15 trillion tokens of data from publicly available sources". The book notes that leaving the composition vague is becoming common.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Compared with the first Transformer's ~4M sentence pairs (maybe ~100M tokens), 15T tokens is a jump of about five orders of magnitude. "Publicly available" says almost nothing about which sites, languages, code or filtering were used.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Even 'open-weights' models may not have open data. Reproducing results, checking for test-set contamination, or understanding biases becomes hard.

terminology.meaning: Releasing a model's parameters does not imply releasing, or even describing, its training data.

paragraphs.excerpt: trained on “15 trillion tokens of data from publicly available sources.” It is
paragraphs.what_it_says: The bullet ends by noting the trend toward vagueness. The sidebar then closes: the next chapter shows how important the exact data mixture is, and when possible you should check where a model's data came from, because it shapes the model's biases and performance.
paragraphs.what_it_means: A model is a compressed reflection of its data. Topics, dialects, viewpoints and errors that are over- or under-represented in pretraining show up in what the model knows and how it behaves, even after fine-tuning.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: For practitioners: when choosing a pretrained backbone, its data provenance is as relevant as its parameter count or benchmark scores, for example whether it saw text in your domain or language.

terminology.meaning: Systematic tendencies in model outputs that reflect skews in the training data.

connections: Chapter 16: the importance of the pretraining data mixture

paragraphs.excerpt: Before we fine-tune our backbone to predict movie reviews, we need to update it
paragraphs.what_it_says: To predict a binary label, the backbone must be extended. It outputs a sequence of shape `(batch_size, sequence_length, 768)`, where each 768-dimensional vector represents an input word in the context of its neighbors. This sequence must be condensed to one vector per sample before predicting a label.
paragraphs.what_it_means: For a batch from p.483 the output is (16, 512, 768): 512 contextual token vectors per review. A sigmoid classifier needs a single (768,) feature vector per review, so some reduction over the sequence axis is required.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This sequence-to-vector reduction is the central design decision when turning any encoder into a classifier, and the backbone does not make it for you (p.481: a backbone is not specialized for any task).
paragraphs.technical_idea: Shapes: $H \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times n \times d}$ with $B=16$, $n=512$, $d=768$ → pooled $h \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times d}$ → logits/probabilities $\in \mathbb{R}^{B \times 1}$.

terminology.meaning: A pretrained model without a task-specific head (p.481).
Layers added on top of a backbone to map its representation to task outputs.

paragraphs.excerpt: One option would be to do mean pooling or max pooling across the whole
paragraphs.what_it_says: Mean or max pooling across the sequence is one option. Using the first token's representation works slightly better: in the final encoder layer the first position can attend to all others and pull information from them, so attention pools contextually instead of coarsely averaging. The authors then add a classification head, including a final `Dense` projection with a nonlinearity before the output.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The `<s>` token carries no meaning of its own, so its final-layer vector is entirely a learned, attention-weighted summary of the review. Fine-tuning trains the attention in the last layers so that this vector collects whatever is useful for sentiment, for example weighting "terrible" heavily and ignoring plot summary. A plain average weights every token equally. Beyond the book: the book says "mean pooling or max pooling ... computing an average", but only mean pooling averages; max pooling takes the per-dimension maximum. Any mean must also skip padding positions using the mask.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It explains the line `x = x[:, 0, :]` in Listing 15.22 (p.485), followed by Dropout, `Dense(768, relu)`, Dropout and a `Dense(1, sigmoid)` output. It also mirrors BERT's convention of a dedicated `[CLS]` token for classification.
paragraphs.technical_idea: First-token pooling: $h = H_{:,0,:}$. Masked mean pooling: $h = \sum_t m_t H_{:,t,:} / \sum_t m_t$. The "contextual" advantage: $H_{:,0,:} = \sum_j \alpha_{0j} v_j$ (plus residual and feedforward), with weights $\alpha_{0j}$ that depend on the content, whereas the mean uses fixed weights $1/n$.

terminology.meaning: Averaging token vectors over the sequence axis.
Taking the maximum of each feature over the sequence axis.
Using the final-layer vector at position 0 as the sequence representation.

p.483: position 0 always holds `<s>` thanks to StartEndPacker

concepts.name: Pretraining data provenance
concepts.definition: Where the text used to pretrain a model comes from, and in what mixture.
concepts.intuition: You are what you read: a model reflects its reading list.
concepts.technical: Growth from ~4M sentence pairs (original Transformer) to Wikipedia + books (BERT), Reddit-linked web pages (GPT-2), and 15T tokens of 'publicly available' data (Llama).
concepts.significance: Shapes model biases and performance; increasingly undisclosed.
concepts.example: A backbone pretrained mostly on English Wikipedia may handle movie-review slang worse than one trained on broad web text.
concepts.misconception: That 'publicly available sources' is a meaningful description of a dataset.

concepts.name: Pooling a sequence into one vector
concepts.definition: Reducing a (batch, sequence_length, d) tensor of token representations to (batch, d) for sequence-level prediction.
concepts.intuition: Summarizing a whole review in one 768-number description.
concepts.technical: Options: mean pooling (masked average), max pooling (per-feature max), or first-token pooling `x[:, 0, :]`, which relies on attention to aggregate information into position 0.
concepts.significance: A required step for classification with an encoder; first-token pooling works slightly better here per the book.
concepts.misconception: That first-token pooling ignores the rest of the review. Through attention, position 0's final vector depends on all positions.

concepts.name: Classification head
concepts.definition: Task-specific layers placed on top of a pretrained backbone to produce predictions.
concepts.intuition: Different screwdriver heads on the same handle (the book's analogy, p.481).
concepts.technical: Here: first-token pooling → Dropout(0.1) → Dense(768, relu) → Dropout(0.1) → Dense(1, sigmoid) (p.485).
concepts.significance: Makes a general backbone answer a specific question (positive vs. negative review).
concepts.example: Fine-tuned on IMDb, the model reaches about 93% test accuracy (p.485).
concepts.misconception: That the head alone is trained. In Listing 15.23 the whole backbone is fine-tuned too, with a small learning rate (5e-5).

concepts.name: Contextual token representation
concepts.definition: Each 768-dimensional backbone output vector represents an input word in the context of its surrounding words.
concepts.intuition: A word's vector is its meaning in this sentence, not in the dictionary.
concepts.significance: These are the features the head builds on.
concepts.example: "not" in "not good" vs. "not bad" contributes differently to the pooled vector.
concepts.misconception: That backbone outputs are word embeddings in the chapter 14 sense.

math.title: Pooling options for the backbone output
math.latex: \begin{aligned} H &\in \mathbb{R}^{B \times n \times 768} \\ h^{\text{first}}_b &= H_{b,0,:} \\ h^{\text{mean}}_b &= \frac{\sum_{t=0}^{n-1} m_{b,t}\, H_{b,t,:}}{\sum_{t=0}^{n-1} m_{b,t}} \\ h^{\text{max}}_{b,k} &= \max_{t:\, m_{b,t}=1} H_{b,t,k} \end{aligned}
math.source_text: (batch_size, sequence_length, 768) ... mean pooling or max pooling across the whole sequence ... using the first token's representation as the pooled value

variables.meaning: backbone output: one 768-d contextual vector per token
sequence length (512 here); here t indexes positions with 0 = <s>
padding mask: 1 for real tokens, 0 for padding (from Listing 15.21)
the pooled 768-d vector for sample b

math.operations: Indexing (first token), masked average, masked per-feature maximum, all over the sequence axis.
math.purpose: Formalizes the three pooling choices the page compares; the book chooses the first one.
math.interpretation: Mean and max use fixed, content-independent aggregation rules; first-token pooling delegates aggregation to the learned attention of the final layer.
math.intuition: Average = everyone gets an equal vote; max = loudest voice per topic; first token = an appointed spokesperson who listened to everyone.
math.numerical_example: Toy case with d = 2 and three real tokens: H = [[0.9, 0.1] (<s>), [0.2, 0.8], [0.4, 0.0]]. First-token: [0.9, 0.1]. Mean: [(0.9+0.2+0.4)/3, (0.1+0.8+0.0)/3] = [0.5, 0.3]. Max: [0.9, 0.8]. If the row of `<s>` resulted from attention weights 0.7 on a strongly negative word, it will lean toward that word's features rather than the average.

deeper.title: Why the first token can act as a summary
deeper.body:
1. StartEndPacker places `<s>` at position 0 of every review (p.483).
2. In every encoder layer, position 0's query attends to all non-padding keys (bidirectional, masked attention), so its vector becomes a weighted mix of the whole review.
3. After 12 layers (p.481), $H_{:,0,:}$ is a deep, content-dependent function of all tokens.
4. During fine-tuning, the gradient from the sentiment loss flows only through position 0's final vector, and that teaches the last layers to route sentiment-relevant information into it.
5. Mean pooling would instead give every token weight $1/n_{\text{real}}$, including neutral plot description.

The book reports that first-token pooling works *slightly* better; it is an empirical choice, and masked mean pooling is a common strong alternative.

deeper.title: Orders of magnitude of pretraining data
deeper.body: Rough scale (beyond the book, approximate): 4M sentence pairs × ~25 tokens per sentence × 2 languages ≈ 2×10^8 tokens; BERT ≈ 3.3×10^9 words; GPT-2 WebText ≈ 40 GB ≈ 10^10 tokens; Llama: 1.5×10^13 tokens. That is roughly a 75,000x increase in about seven years, consistent with the book's "millions → billions → trillions".

visualizations.title: From backbone output to one vector per review
visualizations.why: Shows the reduction described in 15.4.4: (batch, 512, 768) backbone output → first-token pooling → Dense projection → one probability per review (head as in Listing 15.22, p.485).

visualizations.title: Pretraining data scale named in the sidebar (log scale, approximate tokens)
visualizations.why: The sidebar describes growth from millions to trillions of tokens. Only the endpoints (4M sentence pairs, 15T tokens) are given by the book; the token counts for the first two bars are AI estimates for illustration.

misconceptions.claim: Taking only the first token's vector throws away the rest of the review.
misconceptions.correction: Through attention in every layer, the first position gathers information from all other positions; its final vector is a contextual summary.

misconceptions.claim: The `<s>` token's vector is meaningful only because of the word it represents.
misconceptions.correction: `<s>` has no content of its own; its usefulness comes entirely from attention aggregating the sequence, refined by fine-tuning.

misconceptions.claim: Mean pooling over the whole padded sequence is equivalent to averaging the review's tokens.
misconceptions.correction: With 512-length padded inputs, an unmasked mean would mostly average padding; it must use the padding mask (an AI note; the book does not go into this).

misconceptions.claim: Model developers always publish their training data.
misconceptions.correction: The sidebar says it is increasingly secret; Llama's description is just '15 trillion tokens of data from publicly available sources'.

takeaways: Transformer training data grew from millions to trillions of tokens, mostly from the internet.
Examples: ~4M English-German pairs (original Transformer), Wikipedia + 7,000 books (BERT), Reddit-linked pages (GPT-2), 15T tokens (Llama).
Data composition is increasingly undisclosed, yet it shapes a model's biases and performance.
RoBERTa outputs (batch, seq_len, 768); classification requires pooling to one vector per sample.
First-token pooling works slightly better than mean/max pooling because attention lets position 0 gather information contextually.
A Dense projection with a nonlinearity is added before the output (Listing 15.22, p.485).

questions.question: Which pooling strategy do the authors choose for the IMDb classifier, and why?
options: Mean pooling, because it uses every token equally
Max pooling, because it captures the strongest features
The first token's representation, because attention lets that position gather information from the whole sequence contextually
The last token's representation, because it has seen all previous tokens
questions.answer: The first token's representation, because attention lets that position gather information from the whole sequence contextually
questions.explanation: The book says first-token pooling works slightly better than mean/max pooling because position 0 in the final layer attends to all positions. The last-token rationale applies to causal models, not to a bidirectional encoder.

questions.question: What is the shape of the RoBERTa backbone's output, and what does each 768-d vector represent?
questions.answer: (batch_size, sequence_length, 768); each vector represents one input token in the context of its surrounding words.
questions.explanation: Stated in the first paragraph of 15.4.4; consistent with the summary on p.481.

questions.question: According to the sidebar, how was GPT-2's training dataset collected?
options: From English Wikipedia and self-published books
By following outgoing links from Reddit
From 15 trillion tokens of publicly available sources
questions.answer: By following outgoing links from Reddit
questions.explanation: Wikipedia + books is BERT, translation pairs are the original Transformer, and 15T tokens is Llama.

questions.question: Why do the authors advise paying attention to where a model's pretraining data came from?
questions.answer: Because the data shapes the model's biases and performance, and the exact data mixture matters a lot (shown in the next chapter), while companies increasingly keep it vague.
questions.explanation: From the closing paragraph of the sidebar.

questions.question: For a batch of shape (16, 512, 768), what are the output shapes after (a) `x[:, 0, :]` and (b) mean pooling over the sequence axis? How many token vectors does each reduction consider?
questions.answer: (a) (16, 768), reading only position 0 directly (which already mixes all positions through attention). (b) (16, 768), averaging up to 512 vectors per sample (only the unmasked ones if done correctly).
questions.explanation: Both reduce the sequence axis; they differ in how the aggregation weights are determined.

questions.question: Why does first-token pooling make sense for RoBERTa specifically, given the preprocessing on p.483?
questions.answer: StartEndPacker puts `<s>` at position 0 of every review, so the first position is always the same content-free token, whose final vector is purely an attention-built summary of the review.
questions.explanation: Consistent packing guarantees position 0 plays the same role for every sample.

questions.question: Can you list the four example pretraining datasets in chronological order and describe the trend they illustrate?
questions.answer: Original Transformer (4M translation pairs) → BERT (Wikipedia + 7,000 books) → GPT-2 (Reddit-linked web pages) → Llama (15T tokens, vaguely described). Trend: rapidly growing scale, more web scraping, less transparency.
questions.explanation: If you can name the trend in three words (bigger, webbier, vaguer), you have the sidebar's message.
